topic.title: The giveaway that farms you
topic.claim: The iPhone giveaway asking you to follow, tag and share isn't generosity; you're the unpaid growth team.
topic.moment: You tag three friends under a giveaway reel, and so do forty thousand strangers.

turn.believed: A creator is giving away a phone to thank their followers.
turn.actually: One phone buys them tens of thousands of new follows, tags and shares, which is cheaper than any ad.

topic.because: Each entry rule converts you into free reach. The prize is a tiny cost against the followers and spread it manufactures in a week.
topic.payoff: The giveaway where you do all the sharing is the ad where you're the medium.
topic.behaviour: Accounts run follow-tag-share giveaways to cheaply buy reach and followers.
topic.mechanism: Each entry rule turns followers into free distribution worth more than the prize.
topic.send_to: the friend who tags you in every giveaway
topic.why_now: Festive-season giveaways are everywhere right now.

mechanism.broken_premise: The 'permanent follows' sub-claim is the one premise that fails. Giveaway followers churn heavily (a one-year case study of 52 accounts found ~61% unfollow within two weeks of the result), and Meta explicitly demotes follow/like/tag/share 'engagement bait,' so each entry's follow is mostly temporary and the reel's reach is throttled, not amplified. This overstates the per-entrant value but does not overturn the conclusion.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: A giveaway's follow-like-tag-share rules convert each entrant into a distribution node: comment tags fire real notifications, story shares push the post to circles that would never find the account, and even short-lived follows plus the engagement spike cost the organiser nothing but a few taps per person. Across thousands of entrants, buying that same reach and follower volume through ads would cost well more than one ~₹80,000 iPhone, so the aggregate promotional value genuinely exceeds the prize and the single winner is the only paid party, exactly as the post argues. The real-world caveats (most new follows leave, and Meta's algorithm suppresses this kind of bait) shrink the margin and mean much of the 'growth' is vanity, but they do not reverse who is working for whom.

The take's premise is wrong: The conclusion's 'rather than genuine contestants' is a false dichotomy, and the supporting premise that non-winners 'get nothing' is false. A single-prize giveaway with a real draw is a genuine sweepstakes: every valid entry carries a real, positive expected value (prize value ÷ number of entrants), so entrants are simultaneously genuine contestants AND a source of marketing actions. The two are not mutually exclusive, and 'unpaid' overstates it — participants are paid in a lottery ticket priced in effort rather than cash.. How it actually works: A follow/tag/share giveaway is a barter-sweepstakes: the brand swaps a fixed-cost prize and a small chance of winning for engagement actions, buying reach and followers at roughly $0.50–$3 per lead (one case: $1.70 per subscriber), far below paid ads — so yes, the single phone is cheap customer acquisition and the entrants' aggregated actions are the real value. But each entrant is a bona fide contestant in a real draw with non-zero expected value, not merely unpaid staff; the structure is 'contestant who also markets,' not 'marketer instead of contestant.' (Caveat: this holds only when there is an actual draw and real winner — which the post concedes — and much of the reach is weak, since such giveaways see ~30%+ follower churn within a month.) Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

mechanism.broken_premise: Only the 'the follow stays long after the reel is forgotten' sub-claim is overstated — follows are not durable: ~61% of giveaway entrants unfollow within two weeks and 60–80% within 30 days, so the persistent-follow value is largely illusory. Every other premise (comment-tags notify trusted contacts, story shares expose the entrant's circle, the draw is genuine, entrants supply the distribution) holds, and the central claim survives.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Follow + tag-three + story-share is a standard engagement/loop-giveaway growth tactic: the comment mentions fire real notifications to named contacts, the story reshares surface the account to the entrant's followers, and the prize is a one-time cost spread across thousands of unpaid distributors — adjusted cost works out to roughly $0.16–$0.23 per follower, cheap reach bought with entrants' labour rather than ad spend. mechanism.actual_mechanism: A giveaway's follow-like-tag-share rules convert each entrant into a distribution node: comment tags fire real notifications, story shares push the post to circles that would never find the account, and even short-lived follows plus the engagement spike cost the organiser nothing but a few taps per person. Across thousands of entrants, buying that same reach and follower volume through ads would cost well more than one ~₹80,000 iPhone, so the aggregate promotional value genuinely exceeds the prize and the single winner is the only paid party, exactly as the post argues. The real-world caveats (most new follows leave, and Meta's algorithm suppresses this kind of bait) shrink the margin and mean much of the 'growth' is vanity, but they do not reverse who is working for whom.

How it actually works: A follow/tag/share giveaway is a barter-sweepstakes: the brand swaps a fixed-cost prize and a small chance of winning for engagement actions, buying reach and followers at roughly $0.50–$3 per lead (one case: $1.70 per subscriber), far below paid ads — so yes, the single phone is cheap customer acquisition and the entrants' aggregated actions are the real value. mechanism.broken_premise: Only the 'the follow stays long after the reel is forgotten' sub-claim is overstated — follows are not durable: ~61% of giveaway entrants unfollow within two weeks and 60–80% within 30 days, so the persistent-follow value is largely illusory. Every other premise (comment-tags notify trusted contacts, story shares expose the entrant's circle, the draw is genuine, entrants supply the distribution) holds, and the central claim survives.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Follow + tag-three + story-share is a standard engagement/loop-giveaway growth tactic: the comment mentions fire real notifications to named contacts, the story reshares surface the account to the entrant's followers, and the prize is a one-time cost spread across thousands of unpaid distributors — adjusted cost works out to roughly $0.16–$0.23 per follower, cheap reach bought with entrants' labour rather than ad spend. The one correction is durability: most of the followers churn within weeks, so what the prize actually buys is a short burst of entrant-driven reach (matching the post's own 'a week of reach' line) rather than lasting audience, and the 'tag three friends' mechanic sits at the edge of Instagram's own promotion guidelines on tagging. So entrants genuinely are the medium the ad runs on, even if the acquired follows mostly evaporate.

sources.quote: On average, 61% of giveaway participants unfollowed sponsors' accounts within 2 weeks of the giveaway result announcement.
A follower is not a customer. It is not even a lead... Once the giveaway ends, they'll either unfollow your account or turn into 'ghost followers.'
Instagram prohibits tagging content inaccurately or encouraging people to do so... Asking participants to tag a friend in the comments is fine.
